                                      PROJECT NO. 58481




      CHOLLA, INC. RESPONSES TO STAFF DISCUSSION DRAFT 16 TAC §25.194

                                      I. INTRODUCTION

       Cholla, Inc. (“Cholla”) appreciates the opportunity to submit these final comments on the

Commission Staff’s revised discussion draft of proposed 16 TAC §25.194 (Large Load

Interconnection Standards) in Project No. 58481, following the January 9 workshop. Cholla thanks

Commission Staff for the continued engagement with stakeholders and for revising the draft rule

in response to the record developed in this docket.

       Since Cholla submitted its initial comments, ERCOT has publicly announced its intent to

revise its transmission planning process to a Batch Study design. In our earlier filings, Cholla

referred to this evolution as a transition to cluster studies. While the terminology may differ, the

underlying concept is the same: a move away from a strictly linear, project-by-project study

process toward a coordinated planning framework that evaluates groups of large loads together

and develops transmission solutions on a collective basis.

       This announced shift materially affects how several elements of §25.194 will operate in

practice. Requirements related to study sequencing, financial security, treatment of projects that

move forward or drop out, and the identification of necessary transmission upgrades will all

function differently in a Batch Study environment than under today’s linear planning model. As a

result, the final rule must avoid hard-coding assumptions tied exclusively to the current process


                                                                                                  1
 and instead preserve sufficient flexibility to allow the Batch Study framework to develop in

whatever form proves most efficient and effective, while ensuring that §25.194 continues to apply

as intended.

       In these final comments, Cholla has intentionally avoided restating positions set out in our

earlier filings, which we continue to believe provide the most comprehensive and effective path

forward for implementing SB6. Rather than repeat those arguments, these comments focus on the

specific revisions made by Staff, identify areas where Cholla strongly agrees with the revised draft,

and highlight provisions that warrant further adjustment in light of both Staff’s changes and

ERCOT’s announced move toward Batch Studies.

       Cholla evaluates the revised draft consistent with the framework established in our prior

comments under Senate Bill 6 (“SB6”), which requires balancing support for business

development, minimization of stranded infrastructure costs, and maintenance of system reliability.

A final rule that maintains principles-based requirements, rather than narrow process-specific

mandates, will be more durable, more defensible, and better suited to accommodate ERCOT’s

evolving planning methodology without repeated rulemakings.

                                      II. Provisions Cholla Supports

       Cholla supports the following elements of the revised draft, which meaningfully improve

clarity, discipline, and planning effectiveness in the large load interconnection process and are

broadly consistent with SB6’s objectives.

       A. Overall Structure and Use of Defined Interconnection Stages

       Cholla supports the revised draft’s continued use of clearly defined stages—initial

engagement, study execution, intermediate commitments, and final interconnection agreements. A


                                                                                                   2
 staged approach provides transparency to both utilities and customers, creates natural decision

points, and allows commitments to scale appropriately as project certainty increases.

       Importantly, this staged structure appears capable of operating in a Batch Study

environment, provided it is implemented with care. As ERCOT transitions toward Batch Studies,

it will be important that the rule not inhibit the efficient operation of that process by hard-coding

assumptions tied to today’s linear study framework. Requirements related to sequencing,

commitments, and deposits should remain sufficiently flexible to allow Batch Studies to evolve in

whatever form proves most effective, while still preserving the discipline and transparency the rule

is intended to provide. As discussed later in these comments, Cholla has proposed targeted redline

modifications to the revised draft—particularly with respect to deposits and financial

commitments—to better align the rule with this potential reality and avoid unintended constraints

on Batch Study execution.




       B. Clear Timelines and Sequencing in the LLIS Process

       Cholla strongly supports the revised draft’s efforts to impose clearer timelines and

sequencing requirements throughout the Large Load Interconnection Study (“LLIS”) process.

Defined expectations around study initiation, study completion, and subsequent actions provide

meaningful benefits to all participants by reducing uncertainty, discouraging indefinite queue

positions, and improving ERCOT’s ability to rely on study results for transmission planning.

       Clear sequencing is particularly important given the scale and volume of large load requests

now entering the ERCOT system. Without firm timelines and decision points, study results can

quickly become stale, forcing repeated restudies and undermining the usefulness of the planning



                                                                                                   3
 process. The revised draft’s emphasis on moving projects forward—or clearing them out when

commitments are not made—represents a constructive step toward addressing these issues.

       As ERCOT transitions toward a Batch Study planning framework, disciplined sequencing

will become even more critical. In a Batch Study environment, the results of one study cycle are

expected to inform the scope and assumptions of subsequent cycles. That dynamic depends on

timely confirmation of which projects have met required milestones and are genuinely moving

forward. The revised draft’s focus on timelines and sequencing helps create the conditions

necessary for Batch Studies to function effectively, provided those requirements are implemented

in a way that remains adaptable as the Batch Study process evolves.




       C. Removal of Inactive or Stalled Projects

       Cholla strongly supports the revised draft’s provisions addressing inactive or stalled

interconnection requests. Removing projects that are no longer advancing frees transmission

capacity, improves planning model accuracy, and allows ERCOT and the interconnecting utilities

to focus resources on projects that are actively moving toward energization.

       This provision is particularly important in the current environment of rapid large load

growth, where inactive projects can unnecessarily occupy capacity and distort transmission

planning assumptions. Clearing such projects from the queue improves the efficiency of the

interconnection process and supports the timely addition of viable load.

       The removal of inactive or stalled projects will also be essential to the effective operation

of a Batch Study planning framework. Inactive projects carried forward into Batch Studies could




                                                                                                  4
 distort the scope of transmission solutions for an entire group of loads. Ensuring that only

committed projects advance will improve the accuracy and usefulness of Batch Study results.




       D. Dynamic Modeling Requirements

       Cholla supports the revised draft’s requirement that large load customers provide dynamic

modeling data sufficient to allow ERCOT and the interconnecting utility to evaluate system

stability, fault response, and ride-through performance. Accurate dynamic modeling is essential to

maintaining reliability as large loads become a more significant portion of ERCOT demand.

       At the same time, Cholla appreciates that the revised draft does not treat early-stage

dynamic models as fixed compliance certifications. For many large load projects—particularly

data centers and other technology-driven facilities—equipment specifications, control strategies,

and operating characteristics evolve over time. Dynamic models therefore represent the best

available information at a given stage of development and must be capable of being updated as

designs mature.

       This approach is particularly important in a Batch Study environment. As projects progress

through successive study cycles, dynamic modeling assumptions will necessarily be refined based

on updated equipment selections and control configurations. A rule that recognizes the iterative

nature of dynamic modeling will improve study accuracy while avoiding unnecessary restudies or

delays driven by premature attempts to lock in final specifications.

       Cholla therefore supports the revised draft’s dynamic modeling provisions, provided they

continue to recognize dynamic models as iterative planning tools and allow for updates over time

as project information becomes more certain.


                                                                                                5
        E. Disclosure of Substantially Similar Requests (Conceptual Support)

       Cholla supports the revised draft’s continued inclusion of disclosure requirements related

to substantially similar interconnection requests, as such disclosure is expressly contemplated by

SB6 and can provide useful planning transparency for ERCOT and the interconnecting utilities.

       When used appropriately, disclosure of substantially similar requests helps ERCOT and

utilities understand potential interactions among projects and assess whether study assumptions

remain valid as additional requests are submitted. The revised draft’s focus on disclosure—rather

than automatic exclusion or presumption of speculation—remains directionally correct and

consistent with the statute.

       At the same time, Cholla reiterates that similarity in location, size, or developer identity

does not, by itself, indicate that projects are duplicative or speculative. Many large load

development strategies intentionally involve multiple proximate or similarly sized sites for

legitimate technical and commercial reasons, including redundancy, phased deployment, and

architectural design considerations. Properly framed, the disclosure requirement can enhance

planning accuracy without discouraging legitimate development activity.

       Cholla therefore supports the disclosure concept as reflected in the revised draft, while

emphasizing that its application should remain focused on planning transparency and coordination.

Specific concerns regarding definitions, confidentiality, and use of disclosed information are

addressed in later sections of these comments.




                                                                                                 6
        F. Recognition of the Need for Queue Discipline

       Cholla supports the revised draft’s emphasis on improving queue discipline through clearer

milestones, defined consequences for inaction, and more transparent project status management.

In an environment where large load requests are increasing rapidly, effective queue discipline is

essential to maintaining the integrity of the interconnection process and the usefulness of planning

studies.

       Without adequate discipline, projects that are not advancing can continue to occupy

capacity, trigger unnecessary restudies, and distort transmission planning assumptions. The revised

draft appropriately recognizes that meaningful commitments and timely decisions are necessary to

ensure that ERCOT and the interconnecting utilities can rely on study results when developing

transmission solutions.

       Strong queue discipline will be even more important as ERCOT moves toward a Batch

Study planning framework. In a Batch Study environment, the inclusion or exclusion of projects

affects not just individual studies, but the scope and outcome of an entire group of projects

evaluated together. The revised draft’s focus on transparency, milestones, and project status

therefore represents an important foundation for efficient Batch Study execution, provided those

mechanisms are calibrated carefully and applied consistently.

       Cholla supports this direction and views the revised draft’s queue-discipline provisions as

an important step toward a more efficient and reliable interconnection process.

                            III. Provisions Cholla Supports with Refinement

       Cholla supports the overall direction of the revised draft and appreciates the substantial

improvements made by Commission Staff. At the same time, several provisions would benefit


                                                                                                  7
 from further refinement to ensure consistency with SB6’s statutory objectives, cost-causation

principles, and the operational realities of ERCOT’s evolving planning framework.

       In the sections below, Cholla identifies provisions where the revised draft is directionally

correct but would benefit from targeted adjustments. These refinements are intended to preserve

the benefits of the revised draft while avoiding unintended consequences, legal vulnerability, or

constraints on efficient Batch Study execution.

       A. Initial Screening Study

       Cholla understands and appreciates Staff’s objective in introducing an initial screening

study to identify high-level electrical feasibility constraints early in the interconnection process.

Early identification of fundamental deliverability issues can reduce wasted effort and help both

customers and utilities focus resources on viable sites.

       However, Cholla emphasizes that any initial screening study must be explicitly limited in

scope and effect. Early-stage project information is inherently provisional, particularly for large

load projects that may not be developed for several years and where equipment, controls, and site

configurations continue to evolve.

       This limitation is even more pronounced in a Batch Study environment. Under the Batch

Study framework announced by ERCOT, it is anticipated that tens of thousands of megawatts of

new load—potentially in excess of 20,000 MW—may be evaluated together in a single study

cycle. The specific locations of those loads, their relative timing, and the generation resources

developed to serve them will dramatically affect the constraints observed and the transmission

projects ultimately recommended. Those system-wide interactions cannot be meaningfully

predicted in an initial screening study performed on an individual project basis.



                                                                                                   8
        For that reason, initial screening studies have very limited utility in forecasting ultimate

transmission needs or system upgrade costs in a Batch Study paradigm. Where such a screening

study can be helpful is in evaluating the local interconnection path from the point of

interconnection to the load, including identifying whether significant direct-assigned facilities or

CIAC may be required simply to serve the load at its proposed location. In that context, an initial

screening can provide useful information about the minimum level of interconnection cost

exposure, while making clear that total costs identified through subsequent Batch Studies may be

materially higher.

       To be effective and consistent with SB6, an initial screening study should therefore:

   •   be informational and non-binding;

   •   focus solely on high-level electrical feasibility and local interconnection requirements;

   •   avoid requiring early financial security or non-electrical readiness disclosures; and

   •   be clearly distinguished from a Large Load Interconnection Study or facilities

       determination.

       If an initial screening study is treated as a gating mechanism or used to establish system-

level cost responsibility prematurely, it risks discouraging early engagement and undermining

SB6’s objective of supporting business development. Cholla supports the concept of early

screening only if it is implemented narrowly, with clear guardrails, and with explicit recognition

that its results represent a minimum, not comprehensive, view of potential interconnection costs—

particularly in a Batch Study planning framework.

       B. Study Fee Structure




                                                                                                   9
        Cholla supports the revised draft’s inclusion of a flat study fee for large load

interconnection requests, as required by SB6. A minimum study fee provides transparency,

supports cost recovery for ERCOT and the interconnecting utilities, and reinforces the expectation

that interconnection requests reflect a baseline level of seriousness.

       At the same time, Cholla remains concerned that the revised draft’s approach to study fees

may be overly rigid in light of ERCOT’s announced transition to a Batch Study planning

framework. The principal drivers of study cost today—particularly repeated restudies triggered by

incremental changes in system conditions—are closely tied to the current linear planning model.

As planning shifts toward Batch Studies, the nature, timing, and cost drivers of study work are

likely to change materially.

       In a Batch Study environment, ERCOT is expected to assume a greater role in coordinating

studies across large groups of loads and in developing system-level transmission solutions. That

shift may require additional engineering resources, modeling tools, and software capabilities, but

it may also reduce the frequency of project-by-project restudies that currently drive study costs.

Because of these structural changes, it is difficult to conclude that a single set of fixed study-fee

amounts will remain appropriate over time.

       Cholla therefore supports the concept of a flat study fee, but recommends replacing the

revised draft’s reliance on CPI-based adjustments with a process-based approach. Specifically,

Cholla supports establishing a process at ERCOT through which the costs of the study process and

the associated administrative functions are periodically evaluated, including the resources required

on both the ERCOT and Transmission Service Provider sides. That evaluation should inform the

setting of study-fee levels over time, ensuring that fees remain aligned with actual study and

administrative costs as planning methodologies evolve. This approach better reflects the reality of


                                                                                                  10
 a Batch Study framework, where changes in study structure, staffing, and tooling may materially

affect costs in ways that CPI indexing alone cannot capture.

       C. Material Change Definitions

       Cholla appreciates Staff’s effort to provide greater clarity around what constitutes a

“material change” for purposes of large load interconnection requests. Clear guidance can help

reduce unnecessary reporting and provide greater certainty for both customers and utilities.

       At the same time, Cholla emphasizes that materiality should ultimately be determined by

whether a change meaningfully affects ERCOT’s planning assumptions, study results, or the scope

and timing of transmission facilities, rather than by rigid numerical thresholds alone. While

examples such as changes in requested capacity, energization timelines, or point of interconnection

can be useful indicators, they should be treated as illustrative rather than exhaustive.

       Cholla also notes that large load customers require a reasonable degree of surety in the

interconnection process. To make informed investment and development decisions, customers

must be able to understand with clarity when a change will be deemed material and what

consequences may follow. For that reason, whatever framework is adopted should be as clearly

defined as practicable, balancing the need for flexibility with the need for predictable and

transparent application. A rule that is overly vague or entirely discretionary risks creating

uncertainty that can discourage early engagement and efficient project development.

       In a Batch Study environment, the materiality of a given change may depend heavily on

how that change interacts with the broader group of loads being studied. A change that is

immaterial in isolation could become material when considered in combination with other projects,

and vice versa. For that reason, the rule should preserve discretion for ERCOT and the



                                                                                                11
 interconnecting utility to evaluate materiality in context, based on planning relevance, while still

providing customers with sufficient notice of the types of changes that are likely to trigger further

review.

          Cholla supports an approach in which customers are required to notify ERCOT and the

interconnecting utility of changes that could reasonably affect planning outcomes, while avoiding

requirements that force reporting of routine internal adjustments that do not alter electrical

characteristics or study assumptions. Over time, Cholla expects that material change tracking will

be more efficiently handled through ERCOT’s Load Integration and Ongoing Operations (LIOO)

framework, where updates can be assessed dynamically rather than through static rule triggers.

          D. Backup Generation Disclosure

          Cholla supports the revised draft’s requirements for disclosure of backup generation

associated with large load interconnection requests. Visibility into the presence, capacity, and

operating characteristics of backup generation provides ERCOT and the interconnecting utilities

with valuable situational awareness and improves the accuracy of planning and operational

assumptions.

          In particular, understanding backup generation capability allows ERCOT to better assess

how a large load’s net demand at the Point of Interconnection may change under certain operating

conditions, including during system stress events. This information can materially improve

contingency analysis and transmission planning, especially as large loads become a more

significant portion of overall system demand.

          At the same time, Cholla emphasizes that backup generation disclosure should not be

construed as conferring dispatch authority or unilateral operational control over load-owned



                                                                                                  12
 equipment. Reliability challenges related to voltage response or ride-through behavior are system-

level issues that may require a combination of load-side controls, transmission-side solutions, and

coordinated operational strategies. Disclosure supports informed planning and coordination; it

should not, by itself, expand the scope of regulatory or operational authority.

       As with other dynamic project attributes, backup generation information will evolve over

time as site designs mature and equipment selections are finalized. In a Batch Study environment,

where assumptions may be revisited across successive study cycles, it is particularly important that

such information be treated as updateable rather than fixed. Cholla supports migrating ongoing

backup generation updates to ERCOT’s Load Integration and Ongoing Operations (LIOO)

framework as it is implemented, to reduce duplicative filings and ensure ERCOT’s models reflect

current conditions.

       E. Financial Security Deposits

       Cholla supports the use of financial security deposits as a tool to reinforce queue discipline

and ensure that large load interconnection requests reflect a meaningful level of commitment.

Properly designed, security deposits can help protect against stranded infrastructure costs while

providing ERCOT and the interconnecting utilities with greater confidence that projects entering

the study process are capable of moving forward.

       At the same time, Cholla believes the revised draft’s proposed security levels are not

appropriately indexed to anticipated interconnection cost exposure. Financial security should be

calibrated to reasonably expected obligations—including CIAC for direct-assigned facilities

required to physically interconnect the load and securitization of network upgrades identified

through the study process—rather than set at a fixed level that may bear little relationship to actual



                                                                                                   13
 cost risk. Security that materially exceeds likely interconnection cost exposure risks functioning

as an entry barrier rather than as a protective mechanism, which is inconsistent with SB6’s intent.

        Cholla also continues to support a time-differentiated security structure, under which

security requirements decline as the anticipated energization date moves further into the future. As

discussed in Cholla’s original comments and reiterated during the January 9 workshop, a declining

security structure better disciplines interconnection requests by encouraging customers to provide

realistic load ramps, rather than concentrating requested capacity in the first year simply to secure

priority. This approach aligns financial commitment with actual development timelines and

reduces incentives for front-loaded, unachievable ramp profiles.

        A security framework that is indexed to anticipated interconnection costs and that declines

over time as energization is deferred will more effectively balance queue discipline with business

development. Such an approach protects against stranded costs while preserving flexibility for

ERCOT to plan efficiently—particularly as the system transitions toward a Batch Study planning

framework where large groups of projects will be evaluated together.

        F. Cost Allocation, CIAC, and Related Financial Mechanisms

        Cholla remains concerned with several aspects of the revised draft related to cost allocation

and the expanded use of Contributions in Aid of Construction (“CIAC”). While Cholla supports

the principle that large loads should bear costs that are directly attributable to their interconnection,

the revised draft extends CIAC and related mechanisms beyond what is supported by cost-

causation principles, ERCOT’s planning framework, or the record in this docket.

        A. CIAC Must Be Limited to Direct-Assigned Facilities




                                                                                                      14
         Cholla supports the application of CIAC to direct-assigned facilities—facilities that are

required solely to physically interconnect a specific large load at its chosen location. Applying

CIAC in this context is consistent with long-standing practice, aligns with cost causation, and

advances SB6’s objective of minimizing stranded infrastructure costs.

        However, Cholla does not support expanding CIAC to include shared system upgrades

based on “but-for” causation or similar constructs. Under ERCOT’s contingency-based

transmission planning process, the notion of determining a particular load’s “use” of a system

upgrade is inherently arbitrary and, in practice, impossible to calculate in a defensible manner.

        ERCOT planning relies on hundreds to thousands of contingencies to identify the need for

a particular transmission project. Each contingency produces different power flows and different

loading levels across the grid, with individual loads contributing varying amounts to those flows

depending on the scenario. There is no single, stable measure of how much any given load “uses”

a particular facility across the full set of contingencies that justify its construction.

        Moreover, for any identified constraint, there are typically multiple viable transmission

solutions that could resolve the issue. Those alternatives often differ significantly in cost, topology,

and impact on system flows. The ultimate selection among them is driven by engineering

judgment, cost, constructability, and broader system considerations—not by a single load’s

marginal contribution. Assigning cost responsibility based on which option is selected introduces

further arbitrariness, as a different project choice could materially change perceived “usage”

without any change in underlying system need.

        Finally, once a transmission upgrade is constructed, it fundamentally alters system

impedances and flow patterns. In many cases, the predominant users of the new facility are not the



                                                                                                     15
 loads that initially triggered the upgrade, but rather existing loads and resources that now take

advantage of the new transmission path. In such circumstances, attributing the cost of the upgrade

to a single interconnecting load bears little relationship to actual system usage.

       For these reasons, expanding CIAC to shared system upgrades is not merely a policy

disagreement—it is analytically indefensible. There is no non-arbitrary, reproducible method to

assign “use” of a system upgrade across contingencies, project alternatives, and post-construction

system conditions.

       B. Proportional Allocation and Subsequent Compensation Are Unworkable

       The revised draft’s proportional allocation and subsequent compensation mechanisms are

a direct consequence of attempting to solve this analytically impossible problem. Once CIAC is

expanded beyond direct-assigned facilities, the rule necessarily resorts to complex allocation and

reimbursement schemes in an effort to approximate fairness. Those schemes, however, compound

the underlying problem rather than resolving it.

       Determining proportional responsibility for a transmission upgrade across multiple large

loads would require subjective weighting of contingencies, repeated recalculation as system

conditions change, and ongoing tracking as additional loads interconnect or withdraw. This

approach is administratively unworkable and would introduce continual uncertainty into the

interconnection process.

       These constructs also create a first-mover and free-rider problem, in which early

interconnecting loads effectively finance shared infrastructure while later loads—and existing

customers—benefit from the upgrade without corresponding contribution. This outcome conflicts




                                                                                               16
 directly with cost-causation principles and undermines the predictability required for large-scale

investment decisions.

       C. CIAC Is Not a Substitute for System-Wide Cost Allocation

       Cholla further notes that SB6 expressly directed the Commission to examine transmission

cost allocation mechanisms—such as 4CP and TCOS recovery—through separate proceedings.

Expanding CIAC within §25.194 to perform a system-wide cost allocation function is inconsistent

with that statutory direction and risks duplicative or double recovery.

       Shared transmission upgrades should remain system assets, planned through ERCOT’s

regional processes and recovered through established transmission cost allocation mechanisms,

rather than being converted into project-specific obligations through CIAC.

       D. Implications for Batch Study Planning

       These concerns are amplified in a Batch Study environment. Batch Studies are intended to

identify coordinated transmission solutions for groups of loads evaluated together. Applying CIAC

broadly to system upgrades identified through Batch Studies would undermine the purpose of that

framework and reintroduce project-by-project cost allocation challenges that Batch Studies are

designed to eliminate.

       For these reasons, Cholla urges the Commission to revise the cost allocation and CIAC

provisions of the revised draft to:

   •   limit CIAC to direct-assigned facilities,

   •   remove proportional allocation and subsequent compensation constructs, and

   •   preserve system-level planning and cost recovery for shared transmission upgrades.


                                                                                               17
                            IV. Remaining Provisions Cholla Does Not Support

       While the revised draft reflects meaningful progress, several provisions remain

inconsistent with SB6’s statutory objectives, cost-causation principles, and the operational realities

of large load interconnection in ERCOT. Cholla summarizes those concerns below.

       A. Refund Timing and Treatment of Financial Security

       Cholla does not support provisions that require financial security to be held for an extended

period after a project has reached full energization. Once a large load is fully energized, the

associated transmission facilities are in service and the risk of stranded investment has largely been

eliminated. Continuing to hold security beyond that point imposes unnecessary financial burden

without providing corresponding protection.

       Cholla continues to support a refund framework tied to electrical milestones, with full

repayment at or near full energization. This approach aligns financial obligations with actual risk,

supports efficient capital deployment, and remains compatible with both current interconnection

practice and a future Batch Study planning framework.

       B. ERCOT Unilateral Operational Authority Over Loads

       Cholla remains concerned with provisions that would confer broad unilateral authority on

ERCOT to impose ongoing operational standards on large loads beyond emergency conditions or

modeled-behavior assumptions. Reliability challenges such as voltage response and ride-through

performance are system-level issues that typically require coordinated solutions involving

transmission upgrades, control strategies, and market-based services.




                                                                                                   18
        Defaulting to load-only mandates risks oversimplifying complex system interactions and

creates legal and implementation risk. Cholla supports addressing reliability requirements through

established stakeholder processes and cost-causation principles, rather than through unilateral

operational directives embedded in the interconnection rule.

       C. Risk of Overly Rigid Rule Constructs

       Finally, Cholla cautions against adopting rule language that is overly rigid or tightly bound

to today’s planning mechanics. ERCOT’s announced move toward Batch Studies underscores the

need for a rule that enforces discipline and transparency while preserving flexibility to adapt as

planning methodologies evolve.

       Provisions that hard-code assumptions about study sequencing, cost allocation, or

operational authority risk becoming misaligned with future practice and necessitating repeated

rulemakings. A principles-based approach will better serve the Commission, ERCOT, and market

participants over the long term.

                                               V. Conclusion

       Cholla appreciates the significant effort Commission Staff has devoted to revising the

proposed large load interconnection rule and engaging with stakeholders throughout this

proceeding. The revised draft reflects meaningful progress toward improving transparency,

discipline, and planning effectiveness in the face of unprecedented large load growth in ERCOT.

       As reflected in these final comments, Cholla supports many elements of the revised draft

and believes that, with targeted refinements, the rule can fully align with SB6’s co-equal objectives

of supporting business development, minimizing stranded infrastructure costs, and maintaining

system reliability. Where Cholla has recommended changes, those recommendations are intended


                                                                                                  19
 to strengthen the rule’s practical implementation, reduce legal and administrative risk, and ensure

compatibility with ERCOT’s evolving planning framework.

       ERCOT’s announced transition to a Batch Study process underscores the importance of

adopting a rule that is durable and adaptable. Requirements related to study sequencing, financial

commitments, cost allocation, and project treatment must be sufficiently flexible to function

effectively in a coordinated planning environment, while still providing the discipline and certainty

necessary for sound transmission development.

       Cholla remains committed to working collaboratively with Commission Staff, ERCOT,

and other stakeholders to support a large load interconnection framework that enables Texas to

continue leading in advanced computing, data center development, and energy-intensive

industry—without compromising the reliability or efficiency of the ERCOT system. With the

refinements outlined above, §25.194 can serve as a stable and effective foundation for managing

large load interconnection in the years ahead.

2ND DISCUSSION DRAFT
§25.194. Large Load Interconnection Standards.

(a)	Purpose and Scope. This section sets forth the standards and criteria for an electric utility,

a municipally owned utility, and electric cooperative, to interconnect a large load customer

to the ERCOT transmission network.

5

(b)	Definitions. The following words and terms, when used in this section, have the following

meanings unless the context indicates otherwise:

(1)	Backup generating facilities -- Generation facilities that are not capable of

exporting energy to the ERCOT transmission system and that, in aggregate, can

serve at least 50% of on-site contracted peak demand.

(2)	Competitively sensitive information -- Competitively sensitive information

includes exact site locations, such as parcel identifiers or property boundaries;

commercial  terms,  such  as  pricing  or  internal  development  prioritization;

proprietary architectural, operational, or compute-deployment strategies; and

financing structures.	Competitively sensitive information does not include the

identity of a large load customer; load zone; requested or contracted peak demand;

timing of energization; or whether an interconnection request is associated with the

same applicant or affiliated entities.
(3)	Contracted peak demand – the total peak demand that a large load customer
requests that an interconnecting utility serve at a site as stated in an executed and
securitized intermediate agreement or interconnection agreement.


(4)	End-use customer -- the legal entity that eventually will consume the electricity

for its operations at the site subject to an interconnection request, or a corporate

affiliate seeking interconnection on behalf of such legal entity.

(5)	Initial screening study -- A review of current conditions at a site that evaluates

project viability using good engineering judgment without performing a full

interconnection or system impact analysis.

(6)	Interconnecting utility -- The electric utility, municipally owned utility, or electric

cooperative that is certificated to serve the interconnecting large load customer at

retail or, if the certificated utility designates, the interconnecting transmission

service provider.
(7)	Interconnection agreement -- An agreement, executed and securitized by a large
load customer and interconnecting utility after completion of all necessary
transmission studies, that, at a minimum, satisfies subsection (i) of this section.
(8)	Intermediate agreement -- An agreement, executed and securitized by a large load
customer  and  interconnecting  utility  before  completion  of  the large  load
interconnection study, that, at a minimum, satisfies subsection (f) of this section.

(9)	Large load customer -- A customer requesting a new or expanded interconnection

where the customer’s total peak demand at a single site is equal to or exceeds 75

megawatts (MW).

(10)	Large load interconnection study -- a large load interconnection study as that

term is defined in the ERCOT protocols.

(11)	Large load interconnection screening agreement -- An agreement, executed by

                                      I. INTRODUCTION


       Cholla, Inc. ("Cholla") appreciates the opportunity to submit these final comments on the

Commission Staff's revised discussion draft of proposed 16 TAC §25.194 (Large Load

Interconnection Standards) in Project No. 58481, following the January 9 workshop. Cholla thanks

Commission Staff for the continued engagement with stakeholders and for revising the draft rule

in response to the record developed in this docket.


       Since Cholla submitted its initial comments, ERCOT has publicly announced its intent to

revise its transmission planning process to a Batch Study design. In our earlier filings, Cholla

referred to this evolution as a transition to cluster studies. While the terminology may differ, the

underlying concept is the same: a move away from a strictly linear, project-by-project study

process toward a coordinated planning framework that evaluates groups of large loads together

and develops transmission solutions on a collective basis.


       This announced shift materially affects how several elements of §25.194 will operate in

practice. Requirements related to study sequencing, financial security, treatment of proj ects that

move forward or drop out, and the identification of necessary transmi ssion upgrades will all

function differently in a Batch Study environment than under today's linear planning model. As a

result, the final rule must avoid hard-coding assumptions tied exclusively to the current process

 and instead preserve sufficient flexibility to allow the Batch Study framework to develop in

whatever form proves most efficient and effective, while ensuring that §25.194 continues to apply

as intended.

earlier filings, which we continue to believe provide the most comprehensive and effective path

forward for implementing SB6. Rather than repeat those arguments, these comments focus on the

specific revisions made by Staff, identify areas where Cholla strongly agrees with the revised draft,

and highlight provisions that warrant further adjustment in light of both Staff's changes and

ERCOT's announced move toward Batch Studies.

development, minimization of stranded infrastructure costs, and maintenance of system reliability.

A final rule that maintains principles-based requirements, rather than narrow process-specific

mandates, will be more durable, more defensible, and better suited to accommodate ERCOT's

evolving planning methodology without repeated rulemakings.


                                      II. Provisions Cholla Supports


       Cholla supports the following elements of the revised draft, which meaningfully improve

clarity, discipline, and planning effectiveness in the large load interconnection process and are

broadly consistent with SB6's objectives.


       A. Overall Structure and Use of Defined Interconnection Stages


       Cholla supports the revised draft's continued use of clearly defined stages-initial

engagement, study execution, intermediate commitments, and final interconnection agreements. A


                                                                                                    2
 staged approach provides transparency to both utilities and customers, creates natural decision

points, and allows commitments to scale appropriately as proj ect certainty increases.


       Importantly, this staged structure appears capable of operating in a Batch Study

environment, provided it is implemented with care. As ERCOT transitions toward Batch Studies,

it will be important that the rule not inhibit the efficient operation of that process by hard-coding

assumptions tied to today's linear study framework. Requirements related to sequencing,

commitments, and deposits should remain sufficiently flexible to allow Batch Studies to evolve in

whatever form proves most effective, while still preserving the discipline and transparency the rule

is intended to provide. As discussed later in these comments, Cholla has proposed targeted redline

modifications to the revised draft-particularly with respect to deposits and financial

commitments-to better align the rule with this potential reality and avoid unintended constraints

on Batch Study execution.




       B. Clear Timelines and Sequencing in the LLIS Process


       Cholla strongly supports the revised draft's efforts to impose clearer timelines and

sequencing requirements throughout the Large Load Interconnection Study ("LLIS") process.

Defined expectations around study initiation, study completion, and subsequent actions provide

meaningful benefits to all participants by reducing uncertainty, discouraging indefinite queue

positions, and improving ERCOT's ability to rely on study results for transmission planning.


       Clear sequencing is particularly important given the scale and volume of large load requests

now entering the ERCOT system. Without firm timelines and decision points, study results can

quickly become stale, forcing repeated restudies and undermining the usefulness of the planning



                                                                                                   3
 process. The revised draft's emphasis on moving projects forward-or clearing them out when

commitments are not made--represents a constructive step toward addressing these issues.


       As ERCOT transitions toward a Batch Study planning framework, disciplined sequencing

will become even more critical. In a Batch Study environment, the results of one study cycle are

expected to inform the scope and assumptions of subsequent cycles. That dynamic depends on

timely confirmation of which proj ects have met required milestones and are genuinely moving

forward. The revised draft's focus on timelines and sequencing helps create the conditions

necessary for Batch Studies to function effectively, provided those requirements are implemented

in a way that remains adaptable as the Batch Study process evolves.




       C. Removal of Inactive or Stalled Projects


       Cholla strongly supports the revised draft's provisions addressing inactive or stalled

interconnection requests. Removing projects that are no longer advancing frees transmission

capacity, improves planning model accuracy, and allows ERCOT and the interconnecting utilities

to focus resources on proj ects that are actively moving toward energization.


       This provision is particularly important in the current environment of rapid large load

growth, where inactive projects can unnecessarily occupy capacity and distort transmission

planning assumptions. Clearing such projects from the queue improves the efficiency of the

interconnection process and supports the timely addition of viable load.


       The removal of inactive or stalled proj ects will also be essential to the effective operation

of a Batch Study planning framework. Inactive projects carried forward into Batch Studies could




                                                                                                   4
 distort the scope of transmission solutions for an entire group of loads. Ensuring that only

committed projects advance will improve the accuracy and usefulness of Batch Study results.




       D. Dynamic Modeling Requirements


       Cholla supports the revised draft's requirement that large load customers provide dynamic

modeling data sufficient to allow ERCOT and the interconnecting utility to evaluate system

stability, fault response, and ride-through performance. Accurate dynamic modeling is essential to

maintaining reliability as large loads become a more significant portion of ERCOT demand.


       At the same time, Cholla appreciates that the revised draft does not treat early-stage

dynamic models as fixed compliance certifications. For many large load projects-particularly

data centers and other technology-driven facilities-equipment specifications, control strategies,

and operating characteristics evolve over time. Dynamic models therefore represent the best

available information at a given stage of development and must be capable of being updated as

designs mature.


       This approach is particularly important in a Batch Study environment. As projects progress

through successive study cycles, dynamic modeling assumptions will necessarily be refined based

on updated equipment selections and control configurations. A rule that recognizes the iterative

nature of dynamic modeling will improve study accuracy while avoiding unnecessary restudies or

delays driven by premature attempts to lock in final specifications.


       Cholla therefore supports the revised draft's dynamic modeling provisions, provided they

continue to recognize dynamic models as iterative planning tools and allow for updates over time

as project information becomes more certain.

        E. Disclosure of Substantially Similar Requests (Conceptual Support)


        Cholla supports the revised draft's continued inclusion of disclosure requirements related

       When used appropriately, disclosure of substantially similar requests helps ERCOT and

       At the same time, Cholla reiterates that similarity in location, size, or developer identity

does not, by itself, indicate that projects are duplicative or speculative. Many large load

legitimate technical and commercial reasons, including redundancy, phased deployment, and

architectural design considerations. Properly framed, the disclosure requirement can enhance

planning accuracy without discouraging legitimate development activity.


        Cholla therefore supports the disclosure concept as reflected in the revised draft, while

emphasizing that its application should remain focused on planning transparency and coordination.

Specific concerns regarding definitions, confidentiality, and use of disclosed information are

            F. Recognition of the Need for Queue Discipline


           Cholla supports the revised draft's emphasis on improving queue discipline through clearer

milestones, defined consequences for inaction, and more transparent project status management.

In an environment where large load requests are increasing rapidly, effective queue discipline is

essential to maintaining the integrity of the interconnection process and the usefulness of planning

studies.


           Without adequate discipline, proj ects that are not advancing can continue to occupy

capacity, trigger unnecessary restudies, and distort transmission planning assumptions. The revised

draft appropriately recognizes that meaningful commitments and timely decisions are necessary to

ensure that ERCOT and the interconnecting utilities can rely on study results when developing

transmission solutions.


           Strong queue discipline will be even more important as ERCOT moves toward a Batch

Study planning framework. In a Batch Study environment, the inclusion or exclusion of proj ects

affects not just individual studies, but the scope and outcome of an entire group of proj ects

evaluated together. The revised draft's focus on transparency, milestones, and proj ect status

therefore represents an important foundation for efficient Batch Study execution, provided those

mechanisms are calibrated carefully and applied consistently.


           Cholla supports this direction and views the revised draft's queue-discipline provisions as

an important step toward a more efficient and reliable interconnection process.


                               III. Provisions Cholla Supports with Refinement


           Cholla supports the overall direction of the revised draft and appreciates the substantial

improvements made by Commission Staff. At the same time, several provisions would benefit


                                                                                                    7
 from further refinement to ensure consistency with SB6's statutory obj ectives, cost-causation

principles, and the operational realities of ERCOT's evolving planning framework.


       In the sections below, Cholla identifies provisions where the revised draft is directionally

correct but would benefit from targeted adjustments. These refinements are intended to preserve

the benefits of the revised draft while avoiding unintended consequences, legal vulnerability, or

constraints on efficient Batch Study execution.


       A. Initial Screening Study


       Cholla understands and appreciates Staff's obj ective in introducing an initial screening

study to identify high-level electrical feasibility constraints early in the interconnection process.

Early identification of fundamental deliverability issues can reduce wasted effort and help both

customers and utilities focus resources on viable sites.


       However, Cholla emphasizes that any initial screening study must be explicitly limited in

scope and effect. Early-stage project information is inherently provisional, particularly for large

load projects that may not be developed for several years and where equipment, controls, and site

configurations continue to evolve.


       This limitation is even more pronounced in a Batch Study environment. Under the Batch

Study framework announced by ERCOT, it is anticipated that tens of thousands of megawatts of

new load-potentially in excess of 20,000 MW-may be evaluated together in a single study

cycle. The specific locations of those loads, their relative timing, and the generation resources

developed to serve them will dramatically affect the constraints observed and the transmission

projects ultimately recommended. Those system-wide interactions cannot be meaningfully

predicted in an initial screening study performed on an individual proj ect basis.



                                                                                                    8
        For that reason, initial screening studies have very limited utility in forecasting ultimate

transmission needs or system upgrade costs in a Batch Study paradigm. Where such a screening

study can be helpful is in evaluating the local interconnection path from the point of

interconnection to the load, including identifying whether significant direct-assigned facilities or

CIAC may be required simply to serve the load at its proposed location. In that context, an initial

screening can provide useful information about the minimum level of interconnection cost

exposure, while making clear that total costs identified through subsequent Batch Studies may be

materially higher.


       To be effective and consistent with SB6, an initial screening study should therefore:


   •   be informational and non-binding;


   •   focus solely on high-level electrical feasibility and local interconnection requirements;


   •   avoid requiring early financial security or non-electrical readiness disclosures; and


   •   be clearly distinguished from a Large Load Interconnection Study or facilities

       determination.


       If an initial screening study is treated as a gating mechanism or used to establish system-

level cost responsibility prematurely, it risks discouraging early engagement and undermining

SB6's objective of supporting business development. Cholla supports the concept of early

screening only if it is implemented narrowly, with clear guardrails, and with explicit recognition

that its results represent a minimum, not comprehensive, view of potential interconnection Costs-

particularly in a Batch Study planning framework.


       B. Study Fee Structure




                                                                                                   9
        Cholla supports the revised draft's inclusion of a flat study fee for large load

interconnection requests, as required by SB6. A minimum study fee provides transparency,

supports cost recovery for ERCOT and the interconnecting utilities, and reinforces the expectation

that interconnection requests reflect a baseline level of seriousness.


       At the same time, Cholla remains concerned that the revised draft's approach to study fees

may be overly rigid in light of ERCOT's announced transition to a Batch Study planning

framework. The principal drivers of study cost today-particularly repeated restudies triggered by

incremental changes in system conditions-are closely tied to the current linear planning model.

As planning shifts toward Batch Studies, the nature, timing, and cost drivers of study work are

likely to change materially.


       In a Batch Study environment, ERCOT is expected to assume a greater role in coordinating

studies across large groups of loads and in developing system-level transmission solutions. That

shift may require additional engineering resources, modeling tools, and software capabilities, but

it may also reduce the frequency of project-by-project restudies that currently drive study costs.

Because of these structural changes, it is difficult to conclude that a single set of fixed study-fee

amounts will remain appropriate over time.


       Cholla therefore supports the concept of a flat study fee, but recommends replacing the

revised draft's reliance on CPI-based adjustments with a process-based approach. Specifically,

Cholla supports establishing a process at ERCOT through which the costs of the study process and

the associated administrative functions are periodically evaluated, including the resources required

on both the ERCOT and Transmission Service Provider sides. That evaluation should inform the

setting of study-fee levels over time, ensuring that fees remain aligned with actual study and

administrative costs as planning methodologies evolve. This approach better reflects the reality of


                                                                                                  10
 a Batch Study framework, where changes in study structure, staffing, and tooling may materially

affect costs in ways that CPI indexing alone cannot capture.


       C. Material Change Definitions


       Cholla appreciates Staff's effort to provide greater clarity around what constitutes a

"material change" for purposes of large load interconnection requests. Clear guidance can help

reduce unnecessary reporting and provide greater certainty for both customers and utilities.


       At the same time, Cholla emphasizes that materiality should ultimately be determined by

whether a change meaningfully affects ERCOT's planning assumptions, study results, or the scope

and timing of transmission facilities, rather than by rigid numerical thresholds alone. While

examples such as changes in requested capacity, energization timelines, or point of interconnection

can be useful indicators, they should be treated as illustrative rather than exhaustive.


       Cholla also notes that large load customers require a reasonable degree of surety in the

interconnection process. To make informed investment and development decisions, customers

must be able to understand with clarity when a change will be deemed material and what

consequences may follow. For that reason, whatever framework is adopted should be as clearly

defined as practicable, balancing the need for flexibility with the need for predictable and

transparent application. A rule that is overly vague or entirely discretionary risks creating

uncertainty that can discourage early engagement and efficient project development.


       In a Batch Study environment, the materiality of a given change may depend heavily on

how that change interacts with the broader group of loads being studied. A change that is

immaterial in isolation could become material when considered in combination with other projects,

and vice versa. For that reason, the rule should preserve discretion for ERCOT and the



                                                                                                11
 interconnecting utility to evaluate materiality in context, based on planning relevance, while still

providing customers with sufficient notice of the types of changes that are likely to trigger further

review.


          Cholla supports an approach in which customers are required to notify ERCOT and the

interconnecting utility of changes that could reasonably affect planning outcomes, while avoiding

requirements that force reporting of routine internal adjustments that do not alter electrical

characteristics or study assumptions. Over time, Cholla expects that material change tracking will

be more efficiently handled through ERCOT's Load Integration and Ongoing Operations (LIOO)

framework, where updates can be assessed dynamically rather than through static rule triggers.


          D. Backup Generation Disclosure


          Cholla supports the revised draft's requirements for disclosure of backup generation

associated with large load interconnection requests. Visibility into the presence, capacity, and

operating characteristics of backup generation provides ERCOT and the interconnecting utilities

with valuable situational awareness and improves the accuracy of planning and operational

assumptions.


          In particular, understanding backup generation capability allows ERCOT to better assess

how a large load's net demand at the Point of Interconnection may change under certain operating

conditions, including during system stress events. This information can materially improve

contingency analysis and transmission planning, especially as large loads become a more

significant portion of overall system demand.


          At the same time, Cholla emphasizes that backup generation disclosure should not be

construed as conferring dispatch authority or unilateral operational control over load-owned



                                                                                                  12
 equipment. Reliability challenges related to voltage response or ride-through behavior are system-

level issues that may require a combination of load-side controls, transmission-side solutions, and

coordinated operational strategies. Disclosure supports informed planning and coordination; it

should not, by itself, expand the scope of regulatory or operational authority.


       As with other dynamic proj ect attributes, backup generation information will evolve over

time as site designs mature and equipment selections are finalized. In a Batch Study environment,

where assumptions may be revisited across successive study cycles, it is particularly important that

such information be treated as updateable rather than fixed. Cholla supports migrating ongoing

backup generation updates to ERCOT's Load Integration and Ongoing Operations (LIOO)

framework as it is implemented, to reduce duplicative filings and ensure ERCOT's models reflect

current conditions.


       E. Financial Security Deposits


       Cholla supports the use of financial security deposits as a tool to reinforce queue discipline

and ensure that large load interconnection requests reflect a meaningful level of commitment.

Properly designed, security deposits can help protect against stranded infrastructure costs while

providing ERCOT and the interconnecting utilities with greater confidence that proj ects entering

the study process are capable of moving forward.


       At the same time, Cholla believes the revised draft's proposed security levels are not

appropriately indexed to anticipated interconnection cost exposure. Financial security should be

calibrated to reasonably expected obligations-including CIAC for direct-assigned facilities

required to physically interconnect the load and securitization of network upgrades identified

through the study process-rather than set at a fixed level that may bear little relationship to actual



                                                                                                   13
 cost risk. Security that materially exceeds likely interconnection cost exposure risks functioning

as an entry barrier rather than as a protective mechanism, which is inconsistent with SB6's intent.


        Cholla also continues to support a time-differentiated security structure, under which

security requirements decline as the anticipated energization date moves further into the future. As

discussed in Cholla's original comments and reiterated during the January 9 workshop, a declining

security structure better disciplines interconnection requests by encouraging customers to provide

realistic load ramps, rather than concentrating requested capacity in the first year simply to secure

priority. This approach aligns financial commitment with actual development timelines and

reduces incentives for front-loaded, unachievable ramp profiles.


        A security framework that is indexed to anticipated interconnection costs and that declines

over time as energization is deferred will more effectively balance queue discipline with business

development. Such an approach protects against stranded costs while preserving flexibility for

ERCOT to plan efficiently-particularly as the system transitions toward a Batch Study planning

framework where large groups of projects will be evaluated together.


        F. Cost Allocation, CIAC, and Related Financial Mechanisms


        Cholla remains concerned with several aspects ofthe revised draft related to cost allocation

and the expanded use of Contributions in Aid of Construction ("CIAC"). While Cholla supports

the principle that large loads should bear costs that are directly attributable to their interconnection,

the revised draft extends CIAC and related mechanisms beyond what is supported by cost-

causation principles, ERCOT's planning framework, or the record in this docket.


        A. CIAC Must Be Limited to Direct-Assigned Facilities




                                                                                                      14
         Cholla supports the application of CIAC to direct-assigned facilities-facilities that are

required solely to physically interconnect a specific large load at its chosen location. Applying

CIAC in this context is consistent with long-standing practice, aligns with cost causation, and

advances SB6's objective of minimizing stranded infrastructure costs.


        However, Cholla does not support expanding CIAC to include shared system upgrades

based on "but-for" causation or similar constructs. Under ERCOT's contingency-based

transmission planning process, the notion of determining a particular load's "use" of a system

upgrade is inherently arbitrary and, in practice, impossible to calculate in a defensible manner.


        ERCOT planning relies on hundreds to thousands of contingencies to identify the need for

a particular transmission project. Each contingency produces different power flows and different

loading levels across the grid, with individual loads contributing varying amounts to those flows

depending on the scenario. There is no single, stable measure of how much any given load "uses"

a particular facility across the full set of contingencies that justify its construction.


        Moreover, for any identified constraint, there are typically multiple viable transmission

solutions that could resolve the issue. Those alternatives often differ significantly in cost, topology,

and impact on system flows. The ultimate selection among them is driven by engineering

judgment, cost, constructability, and broader system considerations-not by a single load's

marginal contribution. Assigning cost responsibility based on which option is selected introduces

further arbitrariness, as a different project choice could materially change perceived "usage"

without any change in underlying system need.


        Finally, once a transmission upgrade is constructed, it fundamentally alters system

impedances and flow patterns. In many cases, the predominant users of the new facility are not the




                                                                                                     15
 loads that initially triggered the upgrade, but rather existing loads and resources that now take

advantage of the new transmission path. In such circumstances, attributing the cost of the upgrade

to a single interconnecting load bears little relationship to actual system usage.


       For these reasons, expanding CIAC to shared system upgrades is not merely a policy

disagreement-it is analytically indefensible. There is no non-arbitrary, reproducible method to

assign "use" of a system upgrade across contingencies, project alternatives, and post-construction

system conditions.


       B. Proportional Allocation and Subsequent Compensation Are Unworkable


       The revised draft's proportional allocation and subsequent compensation mechanisms are

a direct consequence of attempting to solve this analytically impossible problem. Once CIAC is

expanded beyond direct-assigned facilities, the rule necessarily resorts to complex allocation and

reimbursement schemes in an effort to approximate fairness. Those schemes, however, compound

the underlying problem rather than resolving it.


       Determining proportional responsibility for a transmission upgrade across multiple large

loads would require subj ective weighting of contingencies, repeated recalculation as system

conditions change, and ongoing tracking as additional loads interconnect or withdraw. This

approach is administratively unworkable and would introduce continual uncertainty into the

interconnection process.


       These constructs also create a first-mover and free-rider problem, in which early

interconnecting loads effectively finance shared infrastructure while later loads-and existing

customers-benefit from the upgrade without corresponding contribution. This outcome conflicts




                                                                                               16
 directly with cost-causation principles and undermines the predictability required for large-scale

investment decisions.


        C. CIAC Is Not a Substitute for System-Wide Cost Allocation


        Cholla further notes that SB6 expressly directed the Commission to examine transmission

cost allocation mechanisms-such as 4CP and TCOS recovery-through separate proceedings.

Expanding CIAC within §25.194 to perform a system-wide cost allocation function is inconsistent

with that statutory direction and risks duplicative or double recovery.


        Shared transmission upgrades should remain system assets, planned through ERCOT's

regional processes and recovered through established transmission cost allocation mechanisms,

rather than being converted into project-specific obligations through CIAC.


        D. Implications for Batch Study Planning


        These concerns are amplified in a Batch Study environment. Batch Studies are intended to

identify coordinated transmission solutions for groups of loads evaluated together. Applying CIAC

broadly to system upgrades identified through Batch Studies would undermine the purpose of that

framework and reintroduce project-by-project cost allocation challenges that Batch Studies are

designed to eliminate.


        For these reasons, Cholla urges the Commission to revise the cost allocation and CIAC

provisions of the revised draft to:


    •   limit CIAC to direct-assigned facilities,


    •   remove proportional allocation and subsequent compensation constructs, and


    •   preserve system-level planning and cost recovery for shared transmission upgrades.


                                                                                               17
                             IV. Remaining Provisions Cholla Does Not Support


       While the revised draft reflects meaningful progress, several provisions remain

inconsistent with SB6's statutory obj ectives, cost-causation principles, and the operational realities

of large load interconnection in ERCOT. Cholla summarizes those concerns below.


       A. Refund Timing and Treatment of Financial Security


       Cholla does not support provisions that require financial security to be held for an extended

period after a project has reached full energization. Once a large load is fully energized, the

associated transmission facilities are in service and the risk of stranded investment has largely been

eliminated. Continuing to hold security beyond that point imposes unnecessary financial burden

without providing corresponding protection.


       Cholla continues to support a refund framework tied to electrical milestones, with full

repayment at or near full energization. This approach aligns financial obligations with actual risk,

supports efficient capital deployment, and remains compatible with both current interconnection

practice and a future Batch Study planning framework.


       B. ERCOT Unilateral Operational Authority Over Loads


       Cholla remains concerned with provisions that would confer broad unilateral authority on

ERCOT to impose ongoing operational standards on large loads beyond emergency conditions or

modeled-behavior assumptions. Reliability challenges such as voltage response and ride-through

performance are system-level issues that typically require coordinated solutions involving

transmission upgrades, control strategies, and market-based services.




                                                                                                    18
        Defaulting to load-only mandates risks oversimplifying complex system interactions and

creates legal and implementation risk. Cholla supports addressing reliability requirements through

established stakeholder processes and cost-causation principles, rather than through unilateral

operational directives embedded in the interconnection rule.


       C. Risk of Overly Rigid Rule Constructs


       Finally, Cholla cautions against adopting rule language that is overly rigid or tightly bound

to today's planning mechanics. ERCOT's announced move toward Batch Studies underscores the

need for a rule that enforces discipline and transparency while preserving flexibility to adapt as

planning methodologies evolve.


       Provisions that hard-code assumptions about study sequencing, cost allocation, or

operational authority risk becoming misaligned with future practice and necessitating repeated

rulemakings. A principles-based approach will better serve the Commission, ERCOT, and market

participants over the long term.


                                               V Conclusion


       Cholla appreciates the significant effort Commission Staff has devoted to revising the

proposed large load interconnection rule and engaging with stakeholders throughout this

proceeding. The revised draft reflects meaningful progress toward improving transparency,

discipline, and planning effectiveness in the face of unprecedented large load growth in ERCOT.


       As reflected in these final comments, Cholla supports many elements of the revised draft

and believes that, with targeted refinements, the rule can fully align with SB6's co-equal objectives

of supporting business development, minimizing stranded infrastructure costs, and maintaining

system reliability. Where Cholla has recommended changes, those recommendations are intended


                                                                                                  19
 to strengthen the rule's practical implementation, reduce legal and administrative risk, and ensure

compatibility with ERCOT's evolving planning framework.


       ERCOT's announced transition to a Batch Study process underscores the importance of

adopting a rule that is durable and adaptable. Requirements related to study sequencing, financial

commitments, cost allocation, and proj ect treatment must be sufficiently flexible to function

effectively in a coordinated planning environment, while still providing the discipline and certainty

necessary for sound transmission development.


       Cholla remains committed to working collaboratively with Commission Staff, ERCOT,

and other stakeholders to support a large load interconnection framework that enables Texas to

continue leading in advanced computing, data center development, and energy-intensive

industry-without compromising the reliability or efficiency of the ERCOT system. With the

refinements outlined above, §25.194 can serve as a stable and effective foundation for managing

large load interconnection in the years ahead.
